title: Write-back and stale memory
description: A store under *write-back* changes only the cache. Memory stays stale until the dirty line leaves.

steps.text: This cache is *write-back*: a store changes the line in the cache and sets its dirty bit (D), and memory is not touched. Memory is *stale* for that word until the dirty line is written back. Each set has four ways, so a set holds four lines before it must evict one.
Store 7 to `0x0A4`. Choose Store, type `0x0A4` as the address and 7 as the value, then press Issue.
steps.hint: Switch the operation from Load to Store first; the value box appears next to the address.

steps.text: The line in set 2 is dirty and holds 7. Memory still holds its old value for `0x0A4`, and the memory view marks that word as stale: the cache has a newer value than memory does.
Now change memory directly: edit the word at `0x0A4` in Main memory to 9.
steps.hint: Click the word at `0x0A4` in the memory view, type 9, and press Apply to memory. The editor warns you first.

steps.text: The edit changed memory, but the dirty line still holds 7, so the word is still stale: the cache's copy is the one the program sees. Editing the stale word does not clean the line.
Four more lines map to set 2: `0x1A4`, `0x2A4`, `0x3A4` and `0x4A4`. The set has four ways, so loading all four evicts the dirty line. Once it has left, what does memory hold at `0x0A4`?
options: 7, the value the dirty line held
steps.explain: It holds 7. A dirty line is written back to memory when it leaves, and that overwrites whatever memory held, including your edit.
steps.hint: What happens to a dirty line when it is evicted? Memory must receive its value.

steps.text: Find the write-back: drag the timeline back to step 6.4, the *write-back*, and read memory at `0x0A4`.

The dirty line was written back and memory now holds 7. The stale mark is gone because memory and cache agree again. Only dirty lines cost a write-back; the three clean lines that stayed would have left silently.
